story_text.value:
OpenAI would have you believe you can do real work with Codex.

I have a $20 OpenAI subscription and a $20 Claude subscription.

With Codex I can barely get one meaningful coding task done in the 5h limit. (Either Sol 5.1 high or Astra 6 high.) With Claude I can comfortably get 3 meaningful tasks done. (Opus 5.5 high.)

This is not anecdotal but from repeated experience of dozens of tasks. Doesn't matter what's the size or complexity of those tasks - they're comparable and the differences wash out in the number. I divide my work consistently.

And now an anecdote from a moment ago: I've run out of Opus weekly usage. I've found a bug in my app. Not trivial but not really hard. I had well over 50% of the Codex 5h limit left. I thought: great, Astra will crush this bug in no time. And then I watched as the tokens evaporated and I'm left with half-assed changes. I feel like tearing my hair out. I have to wait till morning to have this solved.

Dear Sam and team: please make your product at least half as competitive as Anthropic's.

title.value: Tell HN: I Hate Codex with Passion

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I wanted to explore how AI models behave when they have their own money. So I gave 4 frontier models their own USDC and had them compete in games of 20 questions. Anyone can watch live.

Each round, one model takes a turn picking the secret word, and the others interrogate it in a group chat.

Every move costs money: 10 cents to ask a question, $1.00 for a wrong guess, and a right guess takes the pot.

Questions are paid for privately, but inform everyone. This introduces a free rider problem that's fun to observe.

The models privately record their best guess and confidence level on every turn. This makes it possible to look for patterns in how they’re calibrated.

Overconfident models bleed money, timid ones rarely win, and well-calibrated ones get rich.

The money is real, and every transfer is on-chain.

At the end of each game a referee model judges the transcript to make sure the host didn’t lie in any answers. If the host is caught lying, it forfeits all its fees (it happens).

Season 1 ran for 85 games and Gemini turned $25 into $61 while Claude and Grok went broke.

Models who had recently guessed wrong were 5x more likely to guess again. Full writeup at https://aquarium.money/twenty/about

Season 2 is live now, and you can watch them play here: https://aquarium.money/twenty

Built solo as a side project.

title.value: Show HN: Four LLMs play 20 questions for real money, live

story_text.value:
I was curious about what classifiers could do. It turns out, a lot, sometimes even play Doom.

Jeffy is currently a collection of simple classifiers that can do spam detection, intent routing, topic classification, sentiment analysis and even play Doom

Jeffy works locally on a regular computer, no GPU needed. It comes with 13 already-trained classifiers, and you can also use Jeffy to train your own classifiers

And there’s a lot that can be built on top of this style of architecture

Curious what tasks people find useful, and what architectures you are using for similar tasks

story_text.value:
I've spent considerable time in my adult life on "choice architecture", meaning ways to coax desired behavior out of myself without exerting willpower. Phone use has been the main concern.

Some things I've tried:

I bought a Kitchen Safe timed box and would leave it in there for hours, sometimes days.

I limited available iPhone apps with iMazing

I hacked together blocking systems in Tasker on a Pixel.

Currently, I'm running a vibe coded blocker app, device owner mode, on the pixel. Works ok, but a fair amount of upkeep and edge cases.

What, if anything, have you tried?

title.value: How do you control your phone use?

story_text.value:
Zebu is a time tracking and invoicing app for freelancers and small teams. It's €5 per seat per month (billed yearly), flat, with no usage fees. There's a limited free plan for solo use.

I built it after 15 years as a solo freelancer on Harvest. After they were acquired, my renewal exploded from $12/month to ~$180/month, and unclear usage based pricing made it hard to predict how much it would always cost. The BBC even reported customers seeing increases of 1,500% - https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/clyq011414eo.

I've been working on a replacement for the past year, and am happy to say my colleagues and I now use it full-time. In many ways it even surpasses the featureset I'd had on Harvest - it's really kind of amazing what kind of custom tooling one can build these days.

I'd especially like feedback on how the migration is working from any services you might come from, any critical integrations that might be useful, and especially what might be missing for team use.

title.value: Show HN: Zebu - time tracking/invoicing for freelancers and small teams

story_text.value:
I ported NHTSA's spVinDecode to TypeScript and run it on Cloudflare Workers over the official monthly vPIC dump, so decoding needs no call to NHTSA (p50 about 1.4 ms).

How it's checked:

It is compared with NHTSA's own SQL functions on the original dump in PostgreSQL. There were 0 unexplained differences on 11,000 VINs. It matches the live API on 95.4% of 1,000 VINs. The rest is newer live data.

While doing this I found that spvindecode in the PostgreSQL dump never applies VinDescriptor overrides. I wrote it up in docs/NHTSA-ERRATA.md.

Limits: only vPIC is fully live. Recalls and fuel economy are partial, and complaints/NCAP are planned. Corgi is a similar project, and I haven't benchmarked against it.

Demo: https://data.ai-kit.net/vpic

title.value: Show HN: Offline NHTSA VIN decoder, verified against NHTSA's own SQL

story_text.value:
This is my first real project; keep in mind I have no formal programming/CS background. It is hand-written; AI was only used for some conceptual questions.

Background: There's an epidemic of "fake" .flac audio files floating around: lossy audio masquerading as true lossless-quality audio. I rewrote the fakeflac.py utility in Go, adding multithreading to greatly improve performance, and increasing portability by embedding an optional WASM build of ffmpeg.

Limitations: the original fakeflac algorithm is a great starting point, but it fails to find a cutoff point with some (obviously very low quality) audio files and produces a false score of 100%. I added CLI flags to tune the cutoff detection, but future versions definitely need some work (less normalization? entirely new detection algorithm?)

title.value: Show HN: Fakeflac-go – A tool for quickly finding "fake" .flac files

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm co-creator of Television (https://television.run/).

Me and the team at Telepath (https://telepath.computer/) have been cooking on this and testing it with a few hundred alpha users. We just opened up the repo to the public today.

Television is a clean, beautiful place for all your artifacts. Think of it as a GUI for your agent harness, a visual space for creating and working with artifacts in collaboration with your agent. It works with any agent harness (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, Pi, OpenCode, etc) and uses whatever inference provider(s) your agent is already using. It's open source.

A CLI and lightweight server get installed wherever your agent harness is running (Linux or macOS for now). These talk to our macOS client app, which can be running anywhere (the browser is also supported with a few limitations). A set of skills tell your agent how to put artifacts on your TV's screen and modify them over time.

You use the client app as a sidecar -- i.e. you chat with your agent the way you normally do, but it can now respond by creating artifacts and putting them on your TV. Everything that ends up on your TV is yours and can be modified by talking to your agent. The entire UI, and your artifacts, are themeable.

We noticed lots of people are using artifacts in agents like Claude Code/Cowork and Codex, and lots of developers are spinning up little websites and webapps for working on projects, organizing their life or work, etc. But it all either ends up locked inside your agent's interface or as a mess of random tabs running on a bunch of ports you quickly lose track of.

We think that the future of personal computer interfaces isn't just chat, any more than it's MS-DOS. Artifacts are an early first step beyond chat. We think they should be easier to work with, and that you should own your own artifacts. So we made Television.

It's early but give it a try and let us know what you think: https://github.com/telepath-computer/television/

(BTW: we're building TV via an end-to-end fully spec-driven dev process, with custom tooling that also pulls in design and UI work. Planning to share more about that in the near future.)

title.value: Show HN: Television – an open source GUI for your agent harness
